title: System for Ensuring the Stable Provision of Specified Critical Infrastructure Services (briefing materials)
date_evidence: As of April 1, 2026, the Cabinet Office Japan has designated a total of 257 specified essential infrastructure service providers under the Economic Security Promotion Act
key_claim: Under the Economic Security Promotion Act's specified-critical-infrastructure system, as of 1 April 2026 the Cabinet Office had designated 257 operators as specified critical infrastructure providers across 15 sectors (electricity, gas, oil, water, railways, freight transport, shipping, ports, aviation, airports, telecommunications, broadcasting, postal services, finance and credit cards); designated operators must file introduction plans and undergo review before installing or outsourcing important equipment, and the regulatory reach extends to the vendors, subcontractors and sub-subcontractors that supply them.
frame_summary: The Cabinet Office documents a standing, expanding regulatory regime that already binds hundreds of infrastructure operators and their supply chains to state review, evidencing that economic security has become permanent administrative machinery rather than an emergency measure.
notes: Primary Japanese-government source for the 257-operator / 15-sector figure (multi-language: Japanese-origin, English briefing PDF). Existence and figure confirmed via WebSearch; numeric provenance for '257' also held in the TIMEWELL record's verbatim_quote. quote_provenance: n/a (no verbatim_quote).

publisher: Advisory Panel on the Economic Security Legal Framework (Cabinet Secretariat, Japan)
title: Recommendations for Further Promotion of Economic Security
date_evidence: The 'Recommendations for Further Promotion of Economic Security' was compiled on January 30, 2026, by the Advisory Panel on the Economic Security Legal Framework housed in the Cabinet Secretariat
key_claim: On 30 January 2026 the Cabinet Secretariat's Advisory Panel on the Economic Security Legal Framework recommended expanding Japan's economic-security regime along three lines: extending support beyond goods to the services indispensable to supplying critical materials (citing submarine cables and rocket launch sites), adding the medical field to critical infrastructure, and using JBIC to finance economically-strategic overseas projects; it also proposed a state economic-security think tank and a public-private council for exchanging sensitive information. These recommendations became the basis for the March 2026 amendment bill.
frame_summary: The advisory panel argues that Japan's economic-security perimeter should be widened from strategic goods to services, medical infrastructure and overseas project finance, and backed by permanent institutions, framing economic security as a standing, expanding state function rather than a one-off response.
notes: Japanese-language primary source (Cabinet Secretariat advisory panel) — satisfies the multi-language sourcing discipline for a Japan-anchored topic. 166 days old, within the soft window. Existence, date and content confirmed via WebSearch and cross-referenced against TIMEWELL's cited footnotes. quote_provenance: n/a (no verbatim_quote).

title: Strategic Comments (2026-15) Caught in the Crossfire: The Weaponization of Economic Interdependence and the Rise of Strategic Litmus Tests
date_evidence: JIIA Strategic Comments (2026-15) ... was published on June 7, 2026, and is available on the JIIA website
key_claim: As interstate competition intensifies, states increasingly mobilise economic instruments for political ends, with measures expanding beyond bilateral relations to extraterritorial application and drawing third states into increasingly institutionalised patterns of coercive economic interaction; these dynamics compel third states to undergo a form of 'strategic litmus test', forcing them to choose which institutional or economic sphere to support.
frame_summary: JIIA argues that the weaponization of economic interdependence is not episodic but is hardening into institutionalised, extraterritorial structures that force third states and firms to pick a side, so economic security is becoming a durable, system-shaping condition rather than a passing dispute.
notes: Global frame anchor (litmus tests / institutionalised coercion). Page fetched; exact publication date (7 June 2026) confirmed via WebSearch and the /2026/06/ URL path. quote_provenance: n/a (no verbatim_quote).

title: Japan's Economic Security Promotion Act Amendment (2026, Cabinet Bill No. 30): What Export Control Officers Should Watch as Services and Medical Infrastructure Come Into Scope
key_claim: On 19 March 2026 the Japanese government approved and submitted Cabinet Bill No. 30, the first substantial amendment to the Economic Security Promotion Act since it was enacted in 2022, revising the Act and the JBIC Act together; its three pillars expand support to services (e.g. submarine cables and rocket launch sites), add the medical field to critical infrastructure, and let JBIC finance strategic overseas projects (semiconductors, shipbuilding, drones). The critical-infrastructure system already covers 15 sectors with 257 designated operators as of 1 April 2026, would move to 16 sectors with medical care, and its review reaches subcontractors and sub-subcontractors.
frame_summary: TIMEWELL argues that Japan's economic-security perimeter is widening from goods to services, medical care and lower supply-chain tiers, and that ordinary companies far from any 'strategic' good will increasingly be pulled into designation, review and screening as the regime keeps adding sectors.
verbatim_quote: as of April 1, 2026, 257 operators are designated as specified critical infrastructure providers
notes: Specialist practitioner explainer grounded in primary sources (Cabinet decision, Diet materials, Cabinet Office briefing, Nikkei), carrying the numeric provenance (257 operators; 15 sectors) used in the body. publisher: Chatham House (The Royal Institute of International Affairs)
title: Saving global economic governance from the 'Trump shock'
key_claim: Chatham House assesses that President Trump's second-term economic policies represent a dramatic break with the past 80 years, that some commentators argue other countries now have no choice but to align economically with either the US or China, and it proposes instead a permanent alliance of market-oriented economies (a 'third pole') built around the EU and the CPTPP economies, without the US or China, to preserve economic openness and the absence of coercion.
frame_summary: Chatham House argues that the fragmentation is a durable, structural break (not a passing phase) and that it is pushing rules-supporting economies toward building permanent new institutions and blocs, corroborating the thesis that economic security is being hard-wired rather than temporarily escalated.
verbatim_quote: some commentators have argued that other countries have no choice but to align themselves economically with either the US or China.
notes: Global/Western frame source for the forced-alignment pressure and the durable, institutionalised response (permanent 'third pole'). title: US International Trade and Investment: Key Shifts in 2025 and What Businesses Should Know for 2026
key_claim: US trade and investment policy has shifted onto a mercantilist, national-and-economic-security footing run largely by executive action: export controls are increasingly used as an economic policy tool alongside their traditional national-security function; the Entity List has been broadened to capture affiliates at least 50% owned by listed entities (implementation suspended one year under a bilateral deal with China); outbound-investment restrictions, Section 232 security tariffs and ICTS supply-chain rules are now standing tools, and companies are being pushed to build multi-tier supply-chain visibility and permanent trade-compliance infrastructure.
frame_summary: Morgan Lewis argues that the US has moved economic security from ad hoc measures to a permanent, expanding compliance environment in which export controls, sanctions and investment screens are standing economic-statecraft tools, so companies must embed trade-compliance and multi-tier supply-chain visibility as durable functions.
verbatim_quote: Export controls are increasingly used as an economic policy tool in addition to their traditional national security function.
notes: US-side structural-framing source, used as the single permitted structural anchor (14 Jan 2026, 182 days, just beyond the soft window and the canonical US year-in-review for the framing). title: Japan approves bill to support overseas projects that can boost economic security
date_evidence: The Japan Times, japan/2026/03/20, 'Japan approves bill to support overseas projects that can boost economic security'
key_claim: In March 2026 Japan's government approved a bill, part of the Economic Security Promotion Act amendment, to support economically-strategic overseas projects, including through JBIC financing, widening the state's economic-security toolkit beyond domestic supply and infrastructure.
frame_summary: The Japan Times reports the March 2026 Cabinet approval as a further extension of Japan's economic-security machinery into overseas project finance, corroborating that the perimeter is widening across the state's economic-statecraft toolkit.
